# Terminology map {#sec-terminology}

Three communities write about searching for evidence, and each has its own words. Information retrieval research says *recall*, *relevance* and *test collection*; evidence-synthesis methods say *sensitivity*, *eligibility* and *reference set*; database documentation says *field tags*, *explode* and *filters*. Often the words name the same thing. Sometimes the same word names different things, which is worse.

This appendix is a crosswalk, not a controlled vocabulary. Usage varies between papers and products, so read each row as a prompt to check what a particular source means. Where a definition comes from a named source, it is cited; otherwise the rows are a practitioner's reading of common usage. The last column points to where the book explains the mechanism.

## Evaluation and units {#sec-terminology-evaluation}

| Concept | Information retrieval | Evidence synthesis | Read in this book |
|---|---|---|---|
| Share of the eligible items found | Recall | Sensitivity [@lefebvre2025, sec. 4.4.3] | @sec-measures-set |
| Share of the found items that are eligible | Precision | Precision; in diagnostic terms, positive predictive value | @sec-measures-set |
| Screening effort per eligible item | (rarely used) | Number needed to read [@bachmann2002] | @sec-measures-set |
| Whether an item counts | Relevance, judged by assessors for an information need | Eligibility, judged against criteria set in a protocol | @sec-missing-relevance |
| The items being counted | Documents | Records, reports and studies, which differ [@page2021] | @sec-missing-units |
| The known eligible items | Relevance judgements, qrels, ground truth | Reference set, gold standard, included studies, benchmark labels | @sec-validation-reference |
| Recall against a partial reference set | Recall against pooled judgements | Relative recall [@sampson2006] | @sec-measures-set |
| A shared evaluation dataset | Test collection | Benchmark (CLEF TAR, SYNERGY) | @sec-validation-benchmarks |
| Items used to build a method, and items kept back to test it | Training and test sets | Development and validation sets [@hausner2012] | @sec-validation-dev |

## Searching databases {#sec-terminology-searching}

The same operations go by different names, and different syntax, on each platform. @sec-boolean-platforms and @sec-dev-system compare the behaviour; this table maps only the names.

| Concept | Common terms | Platform names and syntax | Read in this book |
|---|---|---|---|
| A thesaurus term assigned to records | Subject heading, controlled vocabulary term, descriptor, index term | MeSH heading or descriptor (MEDLINE); Emtree preferred term (Embase); CINAHL Subject Heading | @sec-indexing-headings |
| Other names that lead to a thesaurus term | Synonyms, entry terms | *Entry Terms* in MeSH, *Synonyms* in Emtree [@bramer2018] | @sec-dev-words |
| Including narrower thesaurus terms | Explode, explosion | Default in PubMed (`[mh:noexp]` turns it off); `exp` in Ovid; `/exp` in Embase; `+` in CINAHL, as in `(MH "Primary Health Care+")` [@pubmedhelp; @polyglotreadme] | @sec-dev-system |
| Records where the heading is a main topic | Major topic, focus | `[majr]` in PubMed; *Focus* in Ovid; `/mj`, major focus, in Embase [@ovidmapping; @embasehowsearch] | @sec-indexing-headings |
| The part of a record searched | Field | Field tags (PubMed `[tiab]`, Web of Science `TS=`); field codes (Embase); field suffixes (Ovid `.ti,ab.`) | @sec-dev-translation |
| Matching word endings or internal characters | Truncation, wildcards | The symbols and minimum stem lengths differ by platform | @sec-boolean-platforms |
| Two words near each other | Proximity, adjacency | `adjn` (Ovid), `NEAR/n` (Web of Science, Embase), `W/n` and `PRE/n` (Scopus), `Nn` and `Wn` (EBSCOhost), `[tiab:~n]` (PubMed); what *n* counts differs | @sec-boolean-platforms |
| Rewriting typed words before searching | Query transformation, mapping | Automatic term mapping (PubMed); *Map Term to Subject Heading* (Ovid); broad search (Embase); *Suggest Subject Terms* and expanders (EBSCOhost) | @sec-dev-system |
| Restricting results by a record property | Limits | *Filters* in PubMed's sidebar; *limits* in Ovid | @sec-boolean-not |
| A tested block of terms for a study design or topic | Search filter, hedge | Clinical Queries (PubMed, Ovid) | @sec-indexing-filters |

: Terms for searching bibliographic databases. {#tbl-terminology-searching}

## Screening, stopping and other routes {#sec-terminology-screening}

| Concept | Common terms | Read in this book |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering records so the likely eligible ones are screened first | Screening prioritisation, priority screening, technology-assisted review (TAR), active learning | @sec-stop-order |
| Records labelled before the model's first ranking | Prior knowledge, seed records, starting records | @sec-stop-order |
| Deciding when to stop screening a ranked list | Stopping rule, stopping criterion, stopping heuristic | @sec-stop-heuristics, @sec-stop-statistical |
| Searching from known relevant records | Citation searching, the umbrella term in TARCiS, with backward and forward citation searching and reference list checking [@hirt2024]; also called snowballing or citation chasing | @sec-supp-citation |
| The known records a citation search starts from | Seed references [@hirt2024] | @sec-supp-citation |
| Records like a known one | Similar articles, related articles, more like this | @sec-supp-similarity |
| Running a strategy again | Rerun, rerunning; reproduction, when the aim is the same results; update, when the aim is new records | @sec-recording-rerun, @sec-recording-updating |

## Labels for retrieval methods {#sec-terminology-labels}

Product descriptions name representations, mechanisms, pipeline stages, interfaces and capability claims in the same breath. Before reading a label as an architecture, ask what kind of thing it names.

| Label | What it usually describes | What it does not tell you | Read in this book |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keyword, lexical, full-text search | Matching on analysed words, normally through an inverted index | Whether all words are required, or how results are ordered | @sec-boolean |
| Boolean search | Admission by a logical expression: a record is in or out | Anything about order | @sec-boolean-yes-no |
| Ranked retrieval, relevance sort, Best Match | Records ordered by a score | What evidence the score uses, and how many records can be seen | @sec-ranking |
| Semantic search | A goal: matching meaning beyond literal words | The mechanism, which may be query expansion, learnt representations, reranking or several of these | @sec-representations |
| Vector, embedding or dense retrieval | Records and queries represented as vectors and compared by similarity | What the vectors were trained to capture; vectors need not be learnt or semantic | @sec-representations |
| Hybrid search | Results or signals from two or more routes combined | Which routes, and how they are combined | @sec-pipelines |
| Reranking | A second stage that reorders a shortlist | Anything about records outside the shortlist, which it cannot add | @sec-pipelines |
| Natural-language search | How the query is entered | The backend: the sentence may become a Boolean query, a vector or several searches | @sec-dev-system |
| AI-assisted, AI-powered search | Some machine-learning or generative component | Which stage it affects: the query, retrieval, ranking or the answer | @sec-ranking-ai |
| Retrieval-augmented generation, answer engine | Retrieval supplies records to a model that writes an answer | The retriever, which may be lexical, dense or hybrid | @sec-pipelines |
| Agentic search, deep research | A process that plans, searches repeatedly and follows evidence | Whether each search is lexical or dense, and what was searched | @sec-pipelines |

: Labels for retrieval methods. {#tbl-terminology-labels}

## Words that mean different things in different places {#sec-terminology-overlaps}

**Sensitivity.** In a search, the share of eligible studies retrieved. In a review of diagnostic test accuracy, the share of people with a condition whom the test detects. A search for diagnostic accuracy studies has both, and they are unrelated.

**Test set.** In machine learning, the data kept back to test a model. In @hausner2015, the *test set* is the set used to develop the search strategy, and the records kept back are the *comparator set*; @hausner2012 call them the development and validation sets. Check which is which before comparing figures.

**Pool.** In information retrieval, a *pool* is the set of documents judged for relevance, formed from the top results of the systems being compared; unjudged documents are counted as irrelevant [@zobel1998]. In this book, the *pool* is the set of records a review's own search returned, all carrying the review's screening decisions, as in the CLEF TAR and SYNERGY benchmarks [@kanoulas2019; @debruin2023]. Both kinds of pool miss eligible records outside them, for different reasons.

**Filters.** In evidence synthesis, a *search filter* is a tested block of terms. In PubMed's interface, *Filters* are limits on article type, date or language applied to a result. A strategy can use both, and a report should say which.

**Relevant.** In information retrieval, an assessor's judgement that a document meets an information need. In a review, a record can be relevant to the topic and still ineligible (@sec-missing-relevance). Screening labels record eligibility, usually at two stages, and a "relevant" record in a benchmark is whichever of those the benchmark chose.

**Gold standard.** A reference set treated as complete. It never is: hand-searched sets cover the journals searched, and sets built from reviews' included studies cover what those reviews found [@sampson2006]. *Reference set* is the more honest term.

**Semantic.** A description of a goal, not of a mechanism (@tbl-terminology-labels). A product called semantic may use lexical retrieval with a semantic reranker, or the reverse.
